units.translation: which Hesychius and Eustath. p. 1636, 48 explain as ἀντὶ τοῦ ἐπ᾿ ἄκρον ἤγαγε καὶ τέλος ἐπέθηκε [instead of "he brought to the peak and put an end"]. Correctly the scholion has ἐπὶ ἄκρον ἦλθε [he came to the peak].
But when wretched Orestes had reached the peak of many bloodsheds
instead of "he brought to the peak and put an end"
an army brought in from outside
And he himself raised the war-cry.
And last the Curses raised the shrill war-cry.

in a severely corrupt passage, for which no probable emendation has yet been found. We know the proper name Ἐπάλκης [Epalkes], but the adjective ἐπαλκές [strong], which the scholion explains as ἰσχυροποιόν [strengthening], is nowhere else read: for this reason it was changed by Blomfield to ἐπ᾿ ἀλκῆς [in defense], by Franz to ἐπ᾿ ἀλκᾶς [in defenses], a conjecture not improbable in itself, but uncertain because of the corruption of the neighboring words.
But when the strong grief ... to appear to me well
Rush all to the battlements and gates of the towers.
And a shower of stones comes from the battlements of the defenders.
For there is no battlement of wealth - to obscurity.
in verses of an interpolator. Correctly, as it seems, Auratus has ἐπεμβατῆρας [those who mount upon].
where the highest of evils awaits them to suffer.
The bridle of Zeus compelled him to do these things by force.
to ask again, repeat a question
to ask again, repeat a question
where ἐπανδίπλαζε [he was asking again] is more probable.
He was asking again and learning clearly
I restored for δὲ καλέω Παιᾶνα [but I call upon Paean].
And I invoke in addition the healing Paean, iē
aorist infinitive of ἐπανηρόμην, to ask again
Thus Wellauer for ἐπανέρομαι [I ask again]. In some copies ἐπαναιρόμην [I was asking again], in one ἐπανέρωμαι [I ask again].
I asked you these things again.
to make flowery, adorn with flowers
to make flowery, adorn with flowers. Figuratively, a metaphor drawn from color.
where the scholion has στέφειν ὡς ἄνθεσι [to crown as with flowers].
where Casaubon has ἀπηνθίσω [you plucked off the flowers].
having adorned their race with many toils.
But it is the custom for you to adorn with lamentations a paean
you adorned with much-remembered unwashed blood
having risen from bed as quickly as possible.
and to rise up with white temples to this disease.
I see this man obtaining what he deserves.
I think that from their lovely deep-bosomed breasts they will send forth worthy grief.
and a gift worthy of their evils.
each having what is worthy of justice.
having a white spot on the eye; hence, dim-sighted, obscure
properly said of one who suffers from an eye defect which in Greek is called ἄργεμος [white spot] or λεύκωμα [white film], in Latin albugo. Hence figuratively obscure.
I have made the fiery signs clear, which before were dim.
I am at a loss with obscure oracles.
